name: HGH for height

card.summary: Using growth hormone to try to grow taller; studied in children with short stature, with modest gains, and untested for healthy adults with closed growth plates.
card.aka: growth hormone for height, somatropin, GH, hGH-for-height
card.note: Prescription-only; trials are in children with growth plates open. Evidence for height gain in healthy adults is not available, and long-term risks in healthy adults are described as unknown.

quick.overview:
Human growth hormone (HGH, somatropin) is a prescription injectable used medically for growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic kidney disease, small-for-gestational-age short stature and several other conditions. 'HGH for height' refers to using it, medically or non-medically, to increase height in someone who is short for reasons other than a hormone deficiency, or to try for extra height in the looksmaxxing context.

In clinical trials of children with idiopathic short stature, treatment over several years has been reported to add a few centimetres of adult height on average. Paediatric endocrinology papers debate whether this is meaningful, call it 'cosmetic endocrinology' and discuss cost and ethics. On forums, some users who are past their teenage years ask whether HGH can still add height; no clinical trial identified for this article tests that.
quick.mechanism: Growth hormone acts on the liver and tissues to raise IGF-1 and stimulates growth at the growth plates in the long bones of children and adolescents. Height gain requires open growth plates; after the plates fuse, bones cannot lengthen from growth stimulation. Forum users also talk about growth-hormone-releasing peptides and IGF-1 analogues as alternatives, which are separate and largely unstudied for this purpose.
quick.risks: Documented effects of growth hormone therapy include reduced insulin sensitivity, and some cancer-subgroup signals in large studies. A 2003 editorial cautioned against off-label use and noted that long-term risks in healthy adults are unknown. Forum users report changes such as a widening nose, and cost can be very high. Growth hormone is a prescription drug in most countries, and counterfeit or mislabelled products have been reported in the gray market.

lead: Human growth hormone (HGH), also called somatropin, is a peptide hormone produced by the pituitary gland and available as a recombinant prescription drug. 'HGH for height' refers to using it to increase stature, either in children who are short without a hormone deficiency (so-called idiopathic short stature) or, in looksmaxxing communities, by people who hope to gain height beyond what they would reach naturally.[1][2]

Approved uses described in medical references include growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic kidney failure, Prader-Willi syndrome, intrauterine growth retardation and short-stature homeobox gene deficiency; the FDA approved Humatrope for idiopathic short stature in 2003.[1] Trials in extreme idiopathic short stature reported about 4 to 8 cm of added adult height after roughly four years of treatment, and in Turner syndrome a median gain of about 5 to 8 cm, with gains that appear dose-dependent.[1]

The paediatric literature calls extending growth-hormone treatment to children without deficiency 'cosmetic endocrinology' and recommends restraint, informed assent and cost-conscious practice.[3][4] No clinical trial identified for this article has tested growth hormone for height in healthy adults whose growth plates have closed; a 2003 journal editorial cautioned that long-term risks in healthy adults are unknown.[1]

paras: Growth hormone therapy is approved for children and adults with growth hormone deficiency and for several conditions in which growth is impaired, including Turner syndrome, chronic kidney failure (including around transplant), Prader-Willi syndrome in children, intrauterine growth retardation and short-stature homeobox gene deficiency. It was also approved in 2004 for AIDS-related wasting in adults, and longer-acting weekly formulations were approved in 2020 and 2021.[1]

Idiopathic short stature, meaning extreme short height with no identified cause, is described as one of the most contested indications, since paediatric endocrinologists disagree on how to define it and where to set treatment thresholds. In 2003 the manufacturer Eli Lilly proposed a definition of height more than 2.25 standard deviations below the mean, about the shortest 1.2 per cent of the population.[2]

A randomised trial in 40 girls with Turner syndrome found that height velocity rose from about 3.8 cm per year before treatment to roughly 7.5 to 8 cm per year during the first year of growth hormone with or without low-dose oestrogen.[5] Encyclopedia summaries give median adult height gains of roughly 5 to 8 cm in Turner syndrome and 4 to 8 cm in extreme idiopathic short stature, and note that in chronic kidney failure treatment may narrow a height deficit while a net deficit of around 10 cm can remain.[1]

Authors in Hormone Research in Paediatrics describe the benefit of growth hormone for height in children short for reasons other than deficiency as modest and variable, and say it arose from assumptions about the disability of short stature that now face challenge.[3][4] An encyclopedia entry notes that hormone treatment may not meaningfully improve psychosocial functioning and gives an estimate of costs of $100,000 or more per patient for moving someone from about the 1st to the 10th percentile.[2]

Growth hormone treatment often reduces insulin sensitivity, though some studies found no clear rise in diabetes incidence. A large study found no overall increase in primary cancer risk, with elevated risk in some subgroups, and the FDA's 2011 safety communication called evidence on death risk inconclusive. A small intensive-care trial found higher mortality with growth hormone in critically ill patients.[1]

Editorials in 2003 in the New England Journal of Medicine cautioned against off-label use and noted that long-term risks in healthy adults are unknown.[1] Forum users also describe widening of the nose and other facial changes after prolonged growth hormone use.[9]

Growth hormone was first obtained from human pituitary glands collected at autopsy, coordinated in the US by the National Pituitary Agency from 1960. Supply was scarce and treatment was rationed; about 7,700 US children were treated. In 1985, after four young adults who had received pituitary-derived hormone developed Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, the cadaver-derived product was withdrawn, and Genentech's bacterially produced recombinant product (Protropin) was quickly approved at an initial cost of roughly $10,000 to $30,000 per year.[1]
Growth hormone was part of anabolic-steroid lore in gyms, with counterfeit or fraudulent product reported, and 1990s anti-ageing marketing and internet scams used the 'HGH' label.[1]

Controlled trials exist in children, including a randomised trial of growth hormone with and without oestrogen in Turner syndrome,[5] a phase 3 trial of Saizen in 90 children with idiopathic short stature,[6] a phase 3 trial in 91 children born with serious intrauterine growth retardation,[7] and a not-yet-recruiting phase 3 trial of a Chinese growth hormone injection in idiopathic short stature.[8] Review papers evaluate cost-effectiveness and ethics of 'hGH-for-height'.[3][4]
No studies found of growth hormone for height gain in healthy adults with fused growth plates.

Forum threads include teens and young adults asking whether growth hormone can add an inch or two after a period of using growth-hormone-releasing peptides without noticing height gain, and whether it is too late if growth plate status is unknown.[10] Other posters ask about cycling schedules and routes of administration; the thread replies reflect personal opinions and are not clinical guidance.[11] One poster reports a wider nose after more than a year of use while at 5 foot 8, and asks whether to continue, with replies about suppressing natural production.[9]

timeline.event: US National Pituitary Agency begins coordinating cadaver-derived growth hormone.[1]
Cadaver-derived hormone withdrawn after Creutzfeldt-Jakob cases; recombinant Protropin approved.[1]
FDA approves Humatrope for idiopathic short stature.[1][2]
FDA safety communication calls evidence on death risk inconclusive.[1]
Long-acting weekly growth hormone formulations begin to be approved.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, growth hormone is discussed as a possible way to gain extra height or to continue growth into the late teens, often alongside releasing peptides and IGF-1 analogues.[10]

claims.claim: HGH can still add height even if you are past puberty.
claims.believers: Posters in their late teens ask whether it is too late to 'squeeze out' an inch, and some replies say you might still grow while others say height gain is not possible.[10]
claims.experts: Controlled trials of growth hormone for height are in children with open growth plates; no clinical trial identified for this article has tested it in healthy adults.[1][5][6]

claims.claim: Growth-hormone-releasing peptides (CJC-1295, ipamorelin) or IGF-1 LR3 can substitute for HGH for height.
claims.believers: One user reports using a releasing-peptide combination for about six weeks without noticeable benefit and asks about moving to HGH and IGF-1 LR3, which a reply recommends.[10]
claims.experts: No published trial identified for this article tests these peptides or analogues for height gain in healthy people.

claims.claim: HGH causes facial changes such as a wider nose.
claims.believers: A user reports that his nose became wide after over a year of use and weighs continuing for height against facial change.[9]
claims.experts: Authors of paediatric reviews note that long-term safety of high-dose growth hormone in healthy children is a concern; the sources reviewed here do not specifically document nasal widening in therapy.[3][1]

claims.claim: There is a right way to cycle HGH (on/off schedules, subcutaneous versus intramuscular).
claims.believers: Users trade schedules they have seen and say subcutaneous seems to work better.[11]
claims.experts: Clinical dosing is set by prescribers for medical indications; no published trial identified for this article evaluates cycling schedules for height in healthy people.

claims.claim: Giving growth hormone to normal short children is 'cosmetic endocrinology'.
claims.believers: Not a forum claim; it is the position of some paediatric endocrinology authors who recommend non-treatment for most short children and restraint in enhancing normal adult stature.[3][4]
claims.experts: Reviews call the benefit modest and variable and discuss ethics, cost and fairness.[3][4]
